persons.name: Ali Qasim Salam al-Jaburi

events.description: UN Monitoring Team released its 32nd report on al-Qaeda and the Islamic State
actors: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team

events.description: Episode recorded; hosts note it is almost exactly one year since Zawahiri's killing
Ali Qasim Salam al-Jaburi (Abu Sara al-Iraqi), head of ISIL's General Directorate of Provinces and 'shadow leader', killed
Abu al-Hussein al-Husseini al-Qurashi became emir of the Islamic State
Turkey (Erdogan) claimed ISIL emir Abu al-Hussein had been killed; unconfirmed by ISIL or other states
Abu al-Hasan al-Hashimi al-Qurashi, ISIL emir since February 2022, killed
Abu Ibrahim al-Hashimi al-Qurashi became ISIL emir, serving until February 2022
Turkey announced the detention of Bashar al-Sumaidai, wrongly suggesting he was ISIL's leader
US killed Islamic State of Iraq emir Abu Omar al-Baghdadi and al-Qaeda's representative (Abu Ayyub al-Masri) at ISI's low point
Roggio and Joscelyn debated Peter Bergen on whether al-Qaeda was done, citing al-Qaeda in Iraq's resurgence in Anbar
Roggio testified to the House Homeland Security Committee on global terrorism and al-Qaeda's safe haven in Afghanistan
US killed Ayman al-Zawahiri at a Haqqani guest house in Kabul ('end of July 22'); Taliban still deny it
Iran accused the Taliban of bringing ISIL figures into Afghanistan; Taliban denied it
Pensacola attack, the most recent AQAP projection of a serious threat into the United States
Coup in Niger 'just this week', following coups in Mali and Sudan over the last two years
Previous Generation Jihad episode with Fitton-Brown on the UN Monitoring Team's Afghanistan report (al-Qaeda camps, al-Qaeda leaders in Taliban government)
actors: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team

key_claims: ISIL's General Directorate of Provinces, headed until his February 2023 death by Ali Qasim Salam al-Jaburi (Abu Sara al-Iraqi), had become the real center of gravity of the Islamic State, explaining why successive caliph killings barely affected the group.
Turkey's April 2023 claim to have killed ISIL emir Abu al-Hussein al-Husseini al-Qurashi is unconfirmed; the Monitoring Team is tactfully doubtful and the hosts do not accept he is dead.
Leadership attrition has forced ISIL core to adopt a flat command-and-control structure, trading operational effectiveness for security; ISIL still has 5,000-7,000 members in Iraq and Syria.
Saif al-Adel is al-Qaeda's de facto emir but remains in Iran with Abdul Rahman al-Maghrebi and other seniors; Iran hosts al-Qaeda's most concentrated leadership committee.

al-Qaeda cannot announce Saif al-Adel as emir because doing so would contradict the Taliban's denial that Zawahiri lived and died at a Haqqani guest house in Kabul; the Taliban paid no real price for hosting Zawahiri.
Saif al-Adel's son is inside Yemen in a key AQAP role, giving Saif al-Adel a potential alternative base and influence over AQAP media.
The Haqqani Network maintains strong back channels with Iranian intelligence despite public Iran-Taliban friction.

Roggio rejects the UN assessment that ISKP is the most serious threat in Afghanistan: the Afghan Taliban (which gives state sponsorship to al-Qaeda and TTP) is the biggest threat, then TTP and al-Qaeda, then ISKP; Fitton-Brown agrees TTP outweighs ISKP and warns against CT cooperation with the Taliban.
TTP shelters in Afghanistan and uses an al-Qaeda-run training camp in Kunar province.
The hosts dispute the UN's description of AQAP as 'the most combat ready terrorist group'; al-Shabaab (~$100M/yr revenue, 'Taliban of Africa') is far stronger.

Coups in Mali, Sudan and Niger are turning the Sahelian belt into ungoverned space exploited by JNIM, ISGS and ISWAP; ISIL's Al-Furqan office in northeastern Nigeria may be becoming a financial epicenter.
